f.intro: One shared ban list and whitelist. Bans are permanent and block all IPv4/IPv6 traffic to and from the address, on every connected NS8 node.
f.discovery: The module discovers SSH, the NS8 admin login and installed Gitea, Organizr and Samba instances. A jail reads the login log for its application and identifies the client IP. Every ban applies to all ports and protocols, including forwarded traffic. New applications are checked every minute.
f.threshold: A ban is triggered after 5 matching failed logins within 10 minutes in a jail. It never expires. Samba authentication failure logging is enabled automatically without restarting Samba.
f.afterSetup: Detection sources appear after synchronization is configured.
f.shared: Choose one NS8 module as coordinator. Connect the other NS8 modules to its HTTPS URL with the connection token. The coordinator itself automatically uses the same database.
f.databaseHelp: The SQLite database is included and managed by the module. Only its synchronization service is accessible through HTTPS.
f.proxyHelp: Point this DNS name to this NS8 node. NS8 Traefik handles HTTPS and the certificate automatically.
f.keepSecret: Leave blank to keep the saved token.
f.notifyHelp: Send an ntfy message for a new ban triggered by failed logins on this node. It contains the date, time, jail, node/module and matching log lines. Synchronized bans do not send notifications.
f.whitelistHelp: One address, CIDR network or start–end IP range per line. Saved entries apply on all connected nodes and remove matching bans. Include trusted management, proxy and inter-node addresses here when needed.
f.timeout: The task is still running or timed out. Refresh the page to check its result.
f.taskError: The task failed. Check the task details in NS8 for the exact error.
f.diagnosticsHelp: Connectivity, firewall enforcement, detection and notification delivery are checked separately. During a coordinator outage, existing bans remain active and new local bans wait for synchronization.
f.constraints: Applications write different authentication logs. These parsers are necessary to identify failed logins and their actual client address. They do not restrict which traffic is blocked. A proxy or NAT can hide the original IP: a host firewall can only block addresses visible in the packets. Missing or incompatible logs are reported in Diagnostics.
